# PWR Core Design: Enrichment, Lattice, Moderation, and Reactivity Feedback

Figures below are typical of a Westinghouse-style 4-loop plant (~3400 MWt, 17×17 fuel). Other vendors' designs differ in detail but not in principle.

## Fuel and Enrichment

- **Fuel form:** UO₂ ceramic pellets, ~95% theoretical density, in zirconium-alloy cladding (Zircaloy-4, ZIRLO, or M5).
- **Enrichment:** 3–5 wt% U-235. Reload batches typically run 4.2–4.95%. The US licensing limit has been 5%, and "LEU+" (up to ~8%) is being qualified to support longer cycles and higher burnup.
- **Why low enrichment works:** Light water is a very effective moderator, so a thermal spectrum is reached with modest U-235 content. Higher enrichment mainly buys longer cycles (18–24 months) and higher discharge burnup (~45–60 GWd/tHM).
- **Excess reactivity control:** A fresh core has far more reactivity than needed. Three mechanisms hold it down:
  - **Soluble boron** (boric acid in the coolant): ~1000–2000 ppm at beginning of life, diluted toward ~0 at end of cycle.
  - **Burnable absorbers:** Gd₂O₃ mixed into pellets, or ZrB₂ coatings (IFBA). They burn out as fissile content depletes.
  - **Control rods:** Ag-In-Cd or B₄C. Used for shutdown and power maneuvering, not for long-term reactivity holddown.

## Lattice Geometry (17×17 assembly)

| Parameter | Typical value |
|---|---|
| Rod positions | 289: 264 fuel, 24 guide tubes, 1 instrument tube |
| Fuel rod outer diameter | 9.5 mm |
| Rod pitch | 12.6 mm |
| Pitch-to-diameter ratio (P/D) | ~1.33 |
| Pellet diameter | ~8.2 mm |
| Clad thickness | ~0.57 mm |
| Active fuel height | ~3.66 m (12 ft) |
| Assemblies in core | 193 |
| Coolant conditions | ~15.5 MPa, ~292 °C inlet, ~326 °C outlet |

Pitch is the main design lever on moderation. A tighter pitch means less water per unit of fuel; a looser pitch means more.

## Moderator-to-Fuel Ratio: Deliberately Undermoderated

- The water-to-fuel volume ratio is roughly **1.7–2.0**, which corresponds to a hydrogen-to-heavy-metal atom ratio of about 3.5–4.
- If you plot k∞ against moderator-to-fuel ratio, the curve rises, peaks, and then falls:
  - **Left side (undermoderated):** Neutrons don't thermalize efficiently. More are lost to U-238 resonance capture during slowing down.
  - **Right side (overmoderated):** There is so much water that hydrogen absorption of thermal neutrons dominates.
- **PWRs are designed to sit on the left side of the peak.** Any loss of moderator density reduces reactivity. This covers heatup, boiling, voiding, and a loss of coolant.
- That choice is the root of the negative moderator feedback. A lattice built on the right side of the peak would have a positive moderator coefficient.
- **Soluble boron complicates this.** When the coolant heats and expands, it carries boron out of the core along with the water. Removing an absorber adds reactivity, which pushes the moderator temperature coefficient toward positive. High boron concentration is therefore limited, and burnable absorbers carry part of the holddown instead.

## Reactivity Coefficients

| Coefficient | Typical range | Sign | Response time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fuel temperature (Doppler) | −2 to −5 pcm/K | Always negative | Prompt (fuel heats in milliseconds) |
| Moderator temperature (MTC), beginning of life (BOL), hot full power | ~0 to −20 pcm/K | Must be ≤ 0 at power | Seconds (coolant transit and heat transfer) |
| MTC, end of life (EOL) | −50 to −80 pcm/K | Strongly negative | Seconds |
| Void coefficient | ~ −100 to −200 pcm per % void | Negative | Seconds |
| Power coefficient (combined) | ~ −10 to −25 pcm per % power | Negative | — |
| Pressure coefficient | Small, positive | + | Minor effect |

**Doppler (fuel temperature) feedback**
- Raising the fuel temperature broadens the U-238 absorption resonances.
- Broader resonances capture more neutrons, so reactivity drops.
- This is the first and fastest feedback. It acts before any heat has reached the coolant, which is why it terminates prompt power excursions.

**Moderator temperature feedback (MTC)**
- Hotter water is less dense, so moderation drops. Because the core is undermoderated, reactivity drops too.
- The MTC becomes strongly negative over the cycle for two reasons: boron is diluted out, and plutonium builds up.
- Some technical specifications allow a slightly positive MTC at low power at beginning of life. A non-positive MTC is required at hot full power.

**Delayed neutrons**
- β_eff is about 0.0065 at BOL and falls to about 0.005 at EOL as Pu-239 builds up.
- Delayed neutrons are not a feedback mechanism. They are what make the core controllable: they stretch the effective neutron generation time from microseconds to roughly a tenth of a second or more, so operators and the feedback loops have time to act.

## Why the Core Self-Stabilizes

Suppose power rises.
1. Fuel temperature rises immediately, and Doppler feedback subtracts reactivity.
2. The coolant then heats, its density falls, and the moderator feedback subtracts more.
3. If boiling begins, voids remove moderator, and the void feedback subtracts more still.

Each link pushes back on the original disturbance, so power settles at a new equilibrium instead of running away.

The same feedback makes a PWR **load-following**. When the turbine draws more steam, the coolant cools. A negative MTC turns that cooling into added reactivity, and reactor power rises to meet demand with no rod motion.

The design constraint behind all of this is the requirement for a **negative power coefficient across the whole operating envelope**. That requirement shapes the enrichment, the P/D ratio, the boron limits, and the burnable absorber loading together.
